topics.title: Contextualizing Renaissance and Discovery
skill_responses: Colonization affected Europeans by giving them access to new goods, such as foods, precious metals, and other commercially useful products that enriched European countries and individuals, while also improving European diets. Indigenous peoples were quite adversely affected. European diseases killed countless people who had no resistance. Many more people were killed through warfare and mistreatment. Europeans also damaged indigenous societies by forcing Christianity and European cultures onto these established cultures. African people were stolen from their homes and enslaved to help make European colonization possible.

The shift from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance saw the advent of the Age of Discovery, which affected the European economy when new lands were taken over. The labor of these people (and the enslaved Africans who were brought to the colonies) was used to help produce and export a wide variety of goods that changed and enriched Europe's economy. Within Europe, advances connected to the new thinking of the Renaissance improved farming, created a money economy, and led to the growth of cities and a class of urban merchants and bankers.

topics.title: Italian Renaissance
topics.reflect_question: How did the revival of classical texts contribute to the development of the Italian Renaissance? What were the political, intellectual, and cultural effects of the Italian Renaissance?
topics.reflect_response:
Contribution of Classical Texts | Effects of Classical Texts
The Renaissance was a 'rebirth' of classical ideas—not only in art and architecture but also in writing. Many humanists, including Petrarch, Valla, Ficino, and Pico, studied classical texts intensively. | Political: Machiavelli studied the Roman Republic and wrote the key political text The Prince.
Intellectual: Humanists became more interested in secular ideas and living a good life rather than religion and the afterlife.
Cultural: interest in and respect for ancient texts, including the works of Cicero, Plato, and Aristotle

saq_responses.part_a: Machiavelli argues that leaders should be able to use any action or approach to build and maintain power. Even actions that might be considered unethical are needed and acceptable for a ruler to maintain stability within the state.
saq_responses.part_b: Secular ideas should be the foundation for government. A representative government was the model in classic Rome and Greece. Additionally, morality and religion should be separated from politics.
saq_responses.part_c: Traditional political beliefs were centered around the Roman Catholic Church's conservative and rigid influence on European society. Both Machiavelli and Castiglione's ideas challenged this because they believed that rulers and the aristocracy should conduct themselves based on secular ideals. Guicciardini used his own political experience to write a pessimistic evaluation of how government interacts with individuals.

topics.title: Northern Renaissance
topics.reflect_question: How were Renaissance ideas developed, maintained, and changed as the Renaissance spread to northern Europe?
topics.reflect_response:
Characteristics of the Northern Renaissance | Renaissance Reflected in Religious Reform
Unlike the Italian Renaissance, visual art of the Northern Renaissance tended to be more realistic and more focused on everyday life. Visual artists created works that were physically smaller. Writers focused more on the need for Church reform than their Italian Renaissance counterparts did. | Northern Renaissance writers saw the Church more critically than their counterparts in the Middle Ages had. Erasmus advocated specific reforms for the Church but did not want to split. More envisioned a perfect society and suggested that private property be abolished.

saq_responses.part_a: Students might explain the influence of classicism on the Renaissance by referencing Greek and Roman themes that appear in artwork like Botticelli's Birth of Venus. Students could also demonstrate the inspiration drawn from Roman architecture. For example, the Pantheon impacted the architectural design of Leon Alberti or Filippo Brunelleschi. Students might also reference Leonardo Bruni's On Learning and Literature, which explicitly notes the impact of classicism.
saq_responses.part_b: Students might identify the differences in Italian and Northern Renaissance art. For example, Italian artists focused on idealism and proportion while Northern artists focused on naturalism. A student could also identify the secular nature of the Italian Renaissance versus the role of Christianity in the North.
saq_responses.part_c: Students might identify the similarity in the use of perspective and portraits in both Italian and Northern Renaissance art. Students could identify the importance of individualism and education in both geographic regions. Students could also discuss the role of civic humanism in the courts of Italy and Northern Europe.

saq_responses.part_a: Students might point out one of several ways that the printing press improved the spread of ideas. It made duplication of material faster. Once printers set up the type for a page, they could make several copies quickly. It made copies of printed material less expensive. This made books, pamphlets, reprints of sermons, and other items more accessible to people who were not wealthy. It made copies more accurate. Scribes often introduced mistakes into their work. If a page was set up without mistakes, then every copy would be correct.
saq_responses.part_b: The printing press made copies of the Bible more easily available to common citizens and it spread the ideas of religious reformers such as Martin Luther. Together, these changes weakened the power of the Roman Catholic Church.
saq_responses.part_c: The printing press encouraged the development of vernacular languages by making more items available for people who could not speak or read Latin. However, it also made copies of books in classical Greek and Latin more commonly available for scholars.

topics.title: Causation in the Renaissance and the Age of Discovery
skill_responses: Sample answer: Yes, religion was one of the causes of the Age of Exploration, but it was a secondary cause. The primary cause was to enrich countries through the expansion of trade and the creation of overseas empires. However, the Catholic Church and kingdoms such as Spain and Portugal had a genuine desire to spread Christianity to non-Christians around the world.

Sample answer: The rediscovery of classical ideas was one of the precursors of the Age of Discovery. The knowledge gained and the spirit of inquiry fostered led to advances in seafaring equipment, methods, and capabilities that opened the door to discoveries beyond the narrow seafaring boundaries that the vast majority of Europeans had been limited to. With the Americas and Asia in play, Atlantic nations such as England, the Netherlands, and France were much better placed to engage in exploration, colonization, and seaborne trade.
Sample answer: The establishment of colonies, eventually, provided finances for these new monarchies, helping them solidify their positions against enemies both domestic and foreign.

topics.title: Contextualizing 16th and 17th Century Challenges and Developments
skill_responses: The Protestant Reformation can be seen as a change in that it challenged and broke the dominance of the Roman Catholic Church and set governments and different parts of society on a collision course that previously did not exist. But it can also be seen as a continuity in that it represented the challenge to mainstream Christian thought and administration that was seen in the division of the Orthodox and Catholic churches in the 11th century and the ideas of John Wycliffe, Jan Hus, and others in the 14th and 15th centuries.

The ending of universal Christendom created yet another area of potential conflict between the governments of Europe. It also made space for secular systems of law to take over where religious systems once held sway. This led to tension between secular and religious leaders and between the nobility and monarchies.

historical_perspectives: Many German rulers, including Frederick III of Saxony, supported Luther even if they cared little about theology. They hoped that the religious controversy that Luther caused would weaken the political power of the Roman Catholic Church.

Luther was active during the time of the Northern Renaissance, and he was friends with artists such as Albrecht Dürer. During this period, Germans and other northern Europeans were expressing a distinct culture form southern Europeans.

saq_responses.part_a: A student could note Luther's teaching of ordination as a calling confirmed by the congregation, not a rite performed by the church hierarchy. Students could also explain Luther's view that there were only two sacraments and these could be performed by any believer and did not require ordination. A third possible view that Luther argued was that pastors were not priests and preaching was a ministry not confined to priests.
saq_responses.part_b: Students might defend Luther's support of the structure of the Church by referencing Luther's presence in the Church and his belief that ordination still held a place in the Church's structure. For example, Bainton states Luther's view of the possibility for a minister to hold an office through the commissioning of a congregation. A student might also emphasize Luther's focus on religious practices. For example, Luther argued against the sale of indulgences and against the spiritual authority of the pope and canon law. Luther believed that all spiritual authority resided in the Bible alone (sola scriptura), that salvation (justification) was based on faith alone (sola fide), that works were not necessary for salvation (though works necessarily flowed from true faith), and that ministers could marry. Luther still maintained the institution of the Church and a place for leadership offices to be upheld.
saq_responses.part_c: A student could explain the Roman Catholic Church's 1521 Diet of Worms in which it demanded Luther recant his beliefs. Because Luther refused to recant, he was excommunicated and the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V, declared him an 'outlaw of the empire.' Students could also mention the Leipzig Debate in 1519 where Luther was given a chance to defend his beliefs.

saq_responses.part_a: In the Thirty Years' War, Protestants and Roman Catholics were often fighting one another. The war started with a conflict between the Calvinist ruler Frederick I of Bohemia and the Catholic ruler Ferdinand II of the Holy Roman Empire. During the Danish phase, the Lutheran king of Denmark, Christian IV, fought against the Catholic forces of Ferdinand II. In the Edict of Restitution, Protestants had to return land they had taken from Catholics or pay huge sums of money to them. In the Swedish phase, Protestants under Gustavus Adolphus fought against the Holy Roman Empire's Catholic army.
saq_responses.part_b: France was a mostly Roman Catholic country, but its government, led by Cardinal Richelieu, first supported mostly-Protestant forces led by Gustavus Adolphus and then entered the war directly against the Catholic forces of the Holy Roman Empire.
saq_responses.part_c: The results of the Thirty Years' War had important effects on religion in Europe. In many ways, the war strengthened Protestantism. It ended the idea that Europe would reunite under Roman Catholic leadership. It weakened the Catholic-controlled Holy Roman Empire and recognized the independence of Protestant states such as the Netherlands and the Swiss Confederation. It resulted in countries recognizing Calvinism as an official religion. However, the war also had had important political and economic results, including weakening the Habsburgs and making France the dominant continental power.

topics.title: Causation in the Age of Reformation and the Wars of Religion
skill_responses: The splintering of European Christianity into multiple sects divided the continent because the different groups competed for supremacy. Religious differences quickly became political differences and then military competitions. People's religious convictions were genuine, but political leaders sometimes used religion as a tool to gain influence or expand power.

Urban workers in particular had more options for how to earn a livelihood, becoming lawyers, merchants, or governmental officials. Forms of traditional social control, such as the charivari, began to disappear with the advent of modern justice institutions that developed alongside commercial capitalism. The instability resulting from the breakup of the traditional village economy led to increases in accusations of witchcraft.

The religious wars of Europe had a massive effect on the population of Europe as millions of people died from warfare and related hunger and disease between 1562 and 1648. France experienced nine civil wars in the span of seventeen years in the mid- to late 1500s. Spain's attempts to enforce Catholicism in the Netherlands led to a rebellion and the emergence of the Dutch Republic, which would become a maritime trading powerhouse in the decades that followed. The Thirty Years' War ended up involving most of the countries in Europe and had a massive human toll estimated at three to six million people. From the war, France emerged as the dominant power in Europe, Brandenburg-Prussia emerged as a unified state that would rival Austria, and the power of the Holy Roman Empire was diminished.

topics.title: Contextualizing State Building
skill_responses: States began to move from absolute rulers with centralized power to secular governments that developed new political institutions. Struggles to rule erupted between monarchs who wanted more power and nobles who wanted to maintain their traditional shared power and regional autonomy. Competition between monarchs and nobles became fierce and long-standing.

There began to be challenges to absolute monarchies. Slowly, many people concluded that monarchs did not have a divine right to rule. Instead, they had a social contract with their subjects, in which the ruler had obligations to provide certain rights and security to subjects. At the same time, subjects gave up some freedoms for the protections provided by the monarchy.

topics.title: The English Civil War and the Glorious Revolution
topics.reflect_question: What were the causes and consequences of the English Civil War?
topics.reflect_response:
Causes of the English Civil War | Consequences of the English Civil War
The new Stuart monarchs tried to make England an absolute monarchy. Charles I, like his father, believed he ruled by divine right and argued constantly with Parliament over taxes and other issues. Eventually, civil war broke out between Parliamentarians and Charles's Royalist supporters. | Charles I was executed in 1649.
Oliver Cromwell established a Commonwealth, or republic, and ruled England as lord protector.
Lingering suspicion of Catholic monarchs led to James II being forced to abdicate the throne and his successors required to accept a Bill of Rights.

saq_responses.part_a: The king and Parliament fought over taxes. Since taxes rarely affect all classes equally, this suggests that the war resulted at least in part because of conflicts among class interests.
saq_responses.part_b: Charles I made Parliament suspicious of him through his attempts to unite England with Ireland. If he had been able to achieve his goals without this suspicion or he had stepped back from this effort, he might have avoided the war.
saq_responses.part_c: Both Hill and Masson see the English Civil War as a conflict over the power of the monarchy. However, in these passages, they focus on different aspects of the conflict. Hill takes a broad view: He looks at the large-scale changes in the economy. He sees the English Civil War as a clash between classes. The king was supported by "the reactionary forces of the established Church and conservative landlords." Parliament was supported by "the trading and industrial classes." In contrast, Masson takes a narrow view: She emphasizes the role of one individual, King Charles II. She highlights his "attitude and ineptitude."

saq_responses.part_b: Improvements in sailing technology that made the exploration and colonization of the Americas easier also made trade with Asia safer and more profitable. Improvements in manufacturing technology increased demand for raw materials from abroad and desire for overseas markets in which to sell goods. These changes in technology had wide ramifications. For example, the British involvement in India transformed India from the world's leading producer of textiles and spices into one with a devastated economy.
saq_responses.part_c: For most of the period shown in this table, countries followed the idea of mercantilism, which emphasized maximizing exports. saq_responses.part_b: In response to absolutism, students could describe how the Netherlands didn't have a monarch. The legislative body of the country was the Estates-General, which was made up of provincial leaders, or stadtholders. Additionally, students could describe the development of the Dutch oligarchy, or select ruling class, from the provincial leaders. The urban gentry and rural landholders made up this ruling class.
saq_responses.part_c: Students may note that both states sought to create political stability by removing the power of absolute monarchs. Students could also explain the desire to implement religious tolerance in order to create political stability by ending religious division. Students could address the growing importance of the gentry in both states as the Age of Exploration benefited the urban elite.

saq_responses.part_a: Russia gained the most territory from the partitions. In general, more territory means more people and more resources.
saq_responses.part_b: Before the partitions, Russia and Prussia did not share a border, but after the partitions they did. This might improve trade between them, or it might make them more likely to go to war against each other.
saq_responses.part_c: The partitions eliminated one country that played a role in the balance of power in Europe, and it made three other countries larger and more powerful.

topics.title: Absolutist Approaches to Power
topics.reflect_question: How did absolutist forms of rule affect social and political development from 1648 to 1815?
topics.reflect_response:

historical_perspectives: Students should support their answers with evidence. For example, to emphasize the links between Russia and Western Europe, they might point out that both regions were Christian, and that trade, warfare, and migration connected the two regions. To emphasize differences, they might point out that most Russians were Orthodox while most Western Europeans were Roman Catholic or Protestant, and that most of the land ruled from Moscow was in central or eastern Asia.

Student answers will reflect whether they focus more on the similarities or the differences. Peter instituted changes in technology that used manufacturing, shipping, and the military. However, Russia never developed Western style constitutional monarchy that worked with merchants to promote economic growth. It had a government that was both absolutist and yet too weak to promote.

Historians debate how closely the autocratic regimes of the past and present are related. Some point to a continuity in how Russian leaders have rejected popular participation in government. Others argue that modern governments are more totalitarian (covering more aspects of life) and centralized (keeping more power in Moscow and allowing less for local and regional leaders) than were earlier governments.

saq_responses.part_a: Students could note how monarchs used Baroque artists and architects to create the appearance of power through portraits and grand palaces. For example, the construction of the Palace of Versailles was an example of Louis XIV's grandeur. Students could also reference other examples by absolute monarchs, such as Peter the Great's construction of St. Petersburg, a new capital.
saq_responses.part_b: Students could address the actual power possessed by absolute monarchs by noting the ability of James I of England to dissolve parliament. Students may explain Louis XIV's power to revoke laws such as the Edict of Nantes, or Peter the Great's power to conscript peasants into the military.
saq_responses.part_c: Students may note that new monarchs in the 15th century possessed similar issues as they attempted to consolidate power. For example, Isabella and Ferdinand of Spain were limited by the Cortez, a Spanish assembly made up of nobles. However, this dual monarchy employed the Inquisition to remove the Moors. Students may also note how Louis XI of France desired to create a single dialect of French in order to have better control of the state.

topics.title: Comparison in the Age of Absolutism and Constitutionalism
skill_responses: In an absolute monarchy, one monarch has all the power over a state based on divine right. In a constitutional monarchy, a monarch shares power with a parliament. The monarch rules via a social contract with subjects, not by divine right.

An oligarchy is a legislative body from a select societal class that rules the state. The Dutch oligarchy was made up of rural landholders and urban gentry, or upper-class professionals and merchants. The policies of oligarchs are designed to maintain and increase their status and wealth through trade. Unlike a monarchy, an oligarchy does not have royalty or a parliament.

topics.title: Contextualizing the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment
skill_responses: The Renaissance led philosophers to view critical thinking and classical views as the best means of improving politics, economics, and societies. They believed that applying reason to community problems would produce positive progress and people would become enlightened. European thinkers also applied reason and the scientific method to nature, bringing about the Scientific Revolution.

Enlightenment ideas brought about the printing press and print media and affected public building design. Enlightenment theories on politics and economics evolved to the point of threatening absolutism and mercantilism. The Scientific Revolution brought about a new rational view of religion, which moved people to an appreciation of natural phenomena and calls for religious tolerance.

topics.title: The Scientific Revolution
topics.reflect_question: How did understanding of the natural world develop and change during the Scientific Revolution?

saq_responses.part_a: Stukeley was a close enough acquaintance of Newton's to have dinner and spend time with him. He wrote this passage from the point of view of a friend, rather than a critic, a fellow scientist, or a neutral biographer.
saq_responses.part_b: Stukeley was reporting on an incident that occurred at least 65 years earlier, and his account is based on the memories of two people. Newton had published his theory explaining gravitation in 1687, the year Stukeley was born. So Stukeley is reporting what Newton told him from memory and then Stukeley wrote it down from his memory. Further, Stukeley is reporting on his discussions with one of the most famous men in England.
saq_responses.part_c: Since Stukeley's account was at least 65 years after the event and it relied on both his memory and Newton's, either man might have recalled the event inaccurately. Further, Stukeley might have had an incentive to modify the story to make it more memorable or to enhance his relationship with Newton.

Development of what became known as capitalism from the ideas of Turgot, Quesnay, and Smith

saq_responses.part_a: Students could explain how Enlightenment philosophers were inspired by the ideas of the Scientific Revolution, and some sought rational systems to explain human behavior. For example, rationalism, expounded by Descartes, argued that knowledge could be gained through deductive reasoning.
saq_responses.part_b: Students could refer to Empiricism, promoted by Bacon, which argued that knowledge could be gained through inductive reasoning. Students could also note Montesquieu who proposed a rational structuring of government through the separation of powers. A third answer could describe Deism, a belief that came about as scientific principles were applied to religion in order to make belief in a supreme being rational and logical.
saq_responses.part_c: In spite of the Enlightenment, faith continued to be central to the lives of most Europeans. Most people still worshipped a "God" in a church. Students could also explain that despite economic changes that began to occur, many people were left behind by progress. Agricultural progress was limited for the most part, and people still used traditional methods to eke out a living on the land. Women, for the most part, were unable to be seen, or treated, as equals. A third response could refer to the types of government that varied widely across Europe, some with political power still held by a limited number of people.

saq_responses.part_a: Students might explain the decrease in child mortality in Europe during the 18th century as epidemic diseases, such as smallpox and the Black Death, also decreased. saq_responses.part_a: The entire passage focuses on how much people enjoyed the theater. The first line refers to "a love of the theatre is so general." Other phrases that support this idea are the "inclination to act was awakened," that "it [the casting of parts] was all bewitching," that acting was "an untasted pleasure," that putting on part of a play would be "amusing ourselves," and that finding a piece to perform "would please them all."
saq_responses.part_b: "[Edmund] was determined to prevent it, if possible." Edmund's motivation for opposing the plan is not explained in this short excerpt. The following phrase, "though his mother . . . did not evince the least disapprobation" indicates that she was fine with the plan, but it suggests that some older people would not have been.
saq_responses.part_c: This book was published in 1814, during a period when the middle class was growing. As it did, it created a new market for leisure activities, among these was attending the theater. Austen caught the ethos of these changes in her books.

topics.title: Enlightened and Other Approaches to Power
topics.reflect_question: How were political power and religious toleration influenced by Enlightenment thought from 1648 to 1815?
topics.reflect_response:

Catherine the Great of Russia

historical_perspectives: Cary Nederman attributes the spread of religious toleration to political necessity. She points out that early steps toward toleration, such as the Peace of Augsburg (1555) and Edict of Nantes (1598), reflected political decisions, not ones based on an ideological commitment to freedom of thought. She points to writings by Thomas Hobbes and John Locke during the 17th century that supported religious toleration as evidence that the policy was sensible, not the inevitable result of progress.

Mark Koyama focused on how political conditions after the Reformation led to religious toleration. Once a monarch no longer needed the pope's blessing, persecuting heretics became politically irrelevant and economically unwise. They could allow religion to become a private matter. They did not need to expend money and lives trying to enforce religious unity. In addition, as the state became centralized and standardized, rulers found it more efficient and economically advantageous to treat everyone the same, regardless of their faith. Centralization and standardization drove equality and toleration slowly but steadily. Religious toleration was not part of the story of a steady progress in human history nor part of an improvement in human morality. Rather, it was just a practical response to changes in political structures.

saq_responses.part_a: Students might explain the role of deism in the Enlightenment as allowing for religious tolerance. For example, philosophers like Voltaire supported the principle of freedom of speech. Students could also explain how rationalism and empiricism were supported as methods of determining truth instead of religious beliefs espoused by the Catholic Church.
saq_responses.part_b: Students may reference the emergence of Enlightened monarchs in Central and Eastern Europe as a political institution that permitted religious tolerance. For example, Joseph II of Austria instituted the Edict of Tolerance, which permitted tolerance in the Habsburg Empire for Christians and Jews. Students may also explore the emergence of religious tolerance in the Dutch Republic or under English Constitutionalism which protected religion as a private matter.
saq_responses.part_c: Students may identify the intolerance of absolute monarchs such as Louis XIV, who expelled the Huguenots from France and repealed the Edict of Nantes. Another possible response could explore the failed attempt of the Spanish Habsburg to maintain religious control over the Netherlands.

topics.title: Causation in the Age of the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment
skill_responses: Learning the Greek language was encouraged and made it possible to look back to a wide range of classical texts, providing a source of ideas that challenged the medieval European worldview. These classical texts continued to develop and contributed to Europe's Enlightenment period. Enlightenment-era thinkers believed that questioning old ideas and applying classical thought to community problems would produce positive progress.

Traditional patterns of thought from the Middle Ages gave way to rationalism, empiricism, and skepticism, as well as classical knowledge. These changes in viewpoint affected social order, government, and religion. The Scientific Revolution brought about a new rational view of religion, which moved people to an appreciation of natural phenomena and calls for religious tolerance.

topics.title: Contextualizing 18th-Century States
skill_responses: The commercial competition among European states that grew out of world trade resulted in diplomatic crises and warfare over sovereignty of territories.

Romanticism was a reaction against the Enlightenment. Romanticism demonstrated the emotions involved in mass politics and nationalism, which brought about war and revolutions in Europe and its colonies.

 | The Portuguese employed gunboat diplomacy.
 | Nations fought wars for control of trade.

saq_responses.part_a: Dalrymple describes the growth of the British empire. This could be considered part of several historical developments: the rise of global markets, the growth of European sea power, the development of the British East India Company, and the human costs of wealth.
saq_responses.part_b: In the title of Dalrymple's article, "The Original Evil Corporation," the word evil indicates that he has a negative image of the British East India Company. In the passage, he uses words such as violence, brute force, and looted that convey the same message.
saq_responses.part_c: The British empire was similar to those established by the French, Dutch, Spanish, and Portuguese because it also included overseas colonies. It was unlike these others because it dominated India.

topics.title: Britain's Ascendancy

topics.reflect_response:

The War of the Spanish Succession left France weakened economically. | England, the Dutch Republic, and Austria formed the Grand Alliance to block France's plans for expansion.
England and Scotland formally joined to become Great Britain, providing freedom of trade. | The War of the Spanish Succession led to the Peace of Utrecht, which left France weakened politically and forced France to recognize the Protestant succession in England.
As a result of the Seven Years' War, Great Britain was on its way to world dominance. | Great Britain and France vied for control of North America and India in the War of the Austrian Succession.

 | French aggression in North America led to the French and Indian War, in which France lost all of its land east of the Mississippi, plus Canada, to Great Britain.
 | France provided aid that helped Americans gain independence from Great Britain.

saq_responses.part_a: Both the War of the Austrian Succession and the Seven Years' War grew out of the War of the Spanish Succession, and control of Silesia was a key issue. In both, Prussia and Austria were opponents, and Great Britain and France were opponents. Both wars included fighting in Europe, India, and North America.
saq_responses.part_b: One important difference in the two wars was in how the countries were aligned. In the War of the Austrian Succession, France and Prussia were allies, and Britain and Austria were allies. In the Seven Years' War France and Austria were allies, and Britain and Prussia were allies.
saq_responses.part_c: Overall, Great Britain grew more powerful up through 1763, primarily because it had a stronger navy. It consolidated its control of India and, in the Seven Years' War, took control of French land claims in North America. However, France provided crucial support for the American Revolution. The success of this revolution was a major setback for the British.

saq_responses.part_a: Students could contend that the Committee of Public Safety responded to opposition at home by instituting the Reign of Terror, fixing wages and prices, and pursuing a policy of de-Christianization to preserve the ideals of the Revolution. saq_responses.part_b: Students could explain that the ideals promoted in the Constitution of 1793 were never fully implemented. The Committee of Public Safety undermined the ideals of the Revolution by undermining free speech and by arbitrarily arresting and executing even its own leaders, such as Danton. By implementing the Reign of Terror, the Committee of Public Safety caused the executions of thousands of citizens who were deprived of the right to present evidence or to cross-examine witnesses.
saq_responses.part_c: Students could claim that Doyle believed that the Committee of Public Safety never became a functioning government and instead failed in providing the necessary and effective leadership an unstable France needed.

topics.reflect_response:

Other European nations opposed the French Revolution. | Many opponents of the French Revolution in France emigrated.

saq_responses.part_a: Students could point to the bust of Guillaume-Thomas Raynal in the background of J.B. Belley's portrait. A writer who supported the French Revolution, Raynal's presence implies an important connection between the Haitian Revolution and the French Revolution.
saq_responses.part_b: Students could explain how Belley was a leader in the Haitian Revolution, a movement that involved slaves who sought independence and were inspired by the same ideals of the French Revolution. Students could also explain how Napoleon dispatched an army to put down the Haitian Revolution and in 1802 revoked the law that had abolished slavery in France's colonies. In addition, Toussaint L'Ouverture was arrested and sent to a French prison, where he died.
saq_responses.part_c: Students might explain how the freeing of Haitian slaves and the subsequent independence of Haiti threatened Spain's and Britain's hold on their colonies.

topics.title: Napoleon's Rise, Dominance, and Defeat
topics.reflect_question: What were the effects of Napoleon's rule on European social, economic, and political life? What were the nationalist responses in Europe to Napoleon's rule?
topics.reflect_response:

The Civil Code reinforcing revolutionary principles was adopted by many other European nations that were under French control. | People began to feel pride in their cultural heritage and to desire a single political state for that culture.
Prussia abolished serfdom. | Prussian intellectuals called for unity of the German people.
Prussia instituted military reforms, including a larger standing army. | The Burschenschaft movement called for liberal constitutionalism.
historical_perspectives: His Civil Code provided France with a clear, rational, and usually fair legal code. He established a stable civilian administration, ended guilds, and protected freedoms.

He had a taste for rule and a mania for state building. He used repression to reestablish rule of law, setting up spy networks at home. In conquered lands, there were executions without trials, villages were burned, and his opponents were imprisoned.
Answers may vary. His Civil Code forms the basis for many legal systems, and the ideals and values he ingrained remain central to the values of the European Union today.

saq_responses.part_a: He created a system of state-run schools, called lycées, to provide secular education for students, particularly in technical subjects such as math and engineering, to replace the schools run by the Roman Catholic Church.
saq_responses.part_b: Global trade was increasing, so France needed more people who were trained to work in arsenals, ports, and factories. Earlier schools run by religious institutions focused more on preparing students to become members of the clergy.
saq_responses.part_c: The lycées' primary purpose was to indoctrinate an entire generation into the Napoleonic way of thinking, rather than the thinking of the Roman Catholic Church. Napoleon hoped this would make students loyal subjects of the empire.

topics.reflect_response:

Austria, Great Britain, Prussia, and Russia signed a treaty promising to remain allies for 20 years and not to negotiate separately. | The Congress of Vienna: Redrew the map of Europe
The four allies announced that they were fighting Napoleon, not the French people. | Restored old ruling dynasties to power
The Treaty of Paris called for all eight warring nations to meet in Vienna. | Created the German Confederation to replace the Holy Roman Empire
The four allies decided that they should decide the future of the lands Napoleon had conquered. | Established the principle of freedom of navigation on many rivers
 | Issued a declaration condemning the slave trade
 | Established rules for diplomacy

saq_responses.part_a: European states worked together to advance the principle of freedom of navigation on rivers, to criticize the slave trade, and to establish the principle of multilateral diplomacy.
saq_responses.part_b: Historians who supported the spread of democratic and republican forms of government could have criticized the Congress of Vienna because one of its main goals was to restore to power old ruling dynasties, such as the Bourbons in France. Other historians who advocated for nationalism could have criticized how regions were transferred from one empire to another. Austria took over many northern Italian states, including Lombardy-Venetia. Russia seized the Polish Grand Duchy of Warsaw. The Dutch Republic and the Austrian Netherlands (now Belgium) were united as the Netherlands. Sweden took control of Norway. Great Britain claimed control of former French, Spanish, and Dutch colonies, including the islands of Malta and Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and the Cape Colony in what is now South Africa.
saq_responses.part_c: At the end of the first paragraph, Aaslestad makes a connection between the success of the Congress of Vienna with the need for European countries to work together to maintain peace and solve problems: "The challenges that Europe faced in the twentieth century suggest, in fact, that the type of collaborative diplomacy developed at the Vienna Congress remains essential to limit conflict."

topics.title: Romanticism
topics.reflect_question: How and why did the Romantic movement and religious revival challenge Enlightenment thought from 1648 to 1815?
topics.reflect_response:
Changes | How Changes Challenged Enlightenment Thought
Rationalism fell out of favor as people turned to feelings and emotion, and the beauty of nature. | Writers, musicians, and artists abandoned classical forms and produced works that exhibited emotion and an interest in the past.
Religious revival and evangelical movement | There was an emphasis on private revelation, emotion, and the mysteries of the spirit.
Rise of nationalism and mass uprisings | While inspired by Enlightenment ideals and the French Revolution, they were fueled by the emotions and sentiment of the Romantic Movement.

saq_responses.part_a: The Romantic era's emphasis on feeling and intuition fed into a widespread religious revival. The very magnificence of the natural world, many felt, was proof enough of the existence of God. Generally, these revival movements shared a belief in the truth of personal spiritual experience, mysticism as a gateway to ultimate truth, and an emotional yearning for connection with God.
saq_responses.part_b: Deism, atheism, and skepticism demonstrated doubts people had about traditional religious practices, which included public allegiance to an established church. In reaction to these doubts, evangelical faith movements such as Methodism and pietism spread. These movements emphasized the role of individual conscience, voluntary associations of people, and a desire to persuade others to become Christians.
saq_responses.part_c: The anticlericalism of the Enlightenment and the religious persecution during the Revolution were attacks on the authority of the Roman Catholic Church. In reaction, writers such as François-Auguste-René, vicomte de Chateaubriand, and others represented a Catholic revival.

topics.title: Continuity and Change in 18th-Century States
skill_responses: Britain replaced France as the most powerful European state by the end of the 18th century.
The emotional pride in one's cultural heritage and a desire to maintain a political state for that culture caused European states to resist France's attempts to control the European continent.

topics.title: Contextualizing Industrialization and Its Origins and Effects
skill_responses: Advances in manufacturing, transportation, and communications allowed Europe to develop a worldwide economic network, which helped transform its traditional agricultural economy to an industrial economy by the 19th century. Britain's natural resources, together with its social, economic, and political structures, made it ideal for industrial development. Innovations such as new forms of energy, inventions, and ways of organizing human labor resulted in the beginning of the Industrial Revolution, starting with Britain's textile industry.

By the mid-19th century, Britain had achieved industrial dominance in Europe and the world. Industrialization spread to the European continent and America. Continental European governments were more autocratic than Britain's government. When the continent industrialized, military leaders and aristocrats often held power over the process.

topics.title: The Spread of Industry Throughout Europe
topics.reflect_question: What were the factors that influenced the development of industrialization in various parts of Europe from 1815 to 1914?
topics.reflect_response:
Factors | Influence on Industrial Development
Natural resources | Coal and iron powered factories and railroads.
New technologies | Internal combustion engine and steam power led to more energy for machines and businesses. Bessemer process allowed for mass production of steel. Canals and railroads allowed people to transport goods.
Capitalism | Economic structure that allowed businesspeople to build large factories rather than small workshops
Consumerism | Influenced people so they wanted to buy more things
Patents and prizes | Influenced inventors to keep innovating
Middle class | Influenced government in favor of industrialization and free trade; increased demand for goods
Napoleon's reforms | Helped bring industrialization to France

saq_responses.part_a: Students might explain France's delay in industrialization as a direct result of the country's political instability during the French Revolution. France's political turmoil created an unstable economic system. Responses could also identify the lack of capitalistic policies within France, which likely limited patent protection, or the reliance on mercantilism as possible reasons for France's delay in industrialization.
saq_responses.part_b: Students may note Russia's continued reliance on serfdom as a reason for the delay in industrialization in Eastern Europe. For example, Russian tsars like Catherine II or Alexander I did not support industrialization. Responses could also stress the geographical drawbacks of Eastern European countries. For example, the countries lacked raw materials such as coal, which limited their ability to industrialize.
saq_responses.part_c: Students could explain the role of the state in encouraging industrialization. For example, economist leaders like Friedrich List encouraged industrialization for the sake of nationalism. List recognized the need to industrialize in order to compete in the global marketplace, as well as the need to address national economic problems such as poverty. Students could also examine the impact of Prussia's ability to successfully adopt and adapt English inventions.

topics.reflect_question: How did innovations and advances in technology during the Industrial Revolution lead to economic and social changes?
topics.reflect_response:
Innovations and Technological Advances | Effects of Innovations and Technological Advances

Manchester capitalism | Higher standard of living for workers
Telegraph, telephone | Faster communication
Electric grid | 24-hour cycle of work and play

Chemical engineering | Failed businesses, unemployment, instability, tariffs

Zollverein Agreement | Rapid industrialization in parts of what is now Germany

saq_responses.part_a: List was writing in the mid-19th century. By this period, the Industrial Revolution had made England into a great power, and it was spreading through Europe and the United States. In response to the changes in manufacturing methods, governments were becoming more active in shaping economic and social policies.
saq_responses.part_b: List distinguished between "men of theory," such as Adam Smith and his followers who focused on the benefits of free trade, and the "men of practice" who studied history to see which policies led to prosperity for countries. List considered himself in the "men of practice" group because he pointed out that countries such as England became wealthy by following restrictive trade practices before they adopted free trade.
saq_responses.part_c: List provides two examples. Prussia adopted restrictions on trade, and it prospered. The United States also prospered using restrictions on trade, but when it reduced restrictions, it suffered economically.

topics.title: Social Effects of Industrialization
topics.reflect_question: What were the causes and consequences of social developments resulting from industrialization?
topics.reflect_response:
Causes | Consequences

Working class emerged | More men, women, and children worked outside the home; working-class women often worked as domestic servants
Class identities developed | Support for labor unions and mutual aid societies among working class; increased popularity of fraternal organizations among middle-class men
Rural populations dwindled | Increased immigration abroad; dangerous overcrowding in cities

historical_perspectives: Their lifespans lengthened, and they were able to afford more possessions that were of better quality.
Probably not, since people often lied and cheated to get around the laws, and there were few penalties for violators.

saq_responses.part_a: Students can explain that housekeeping, nursing, teaching, and social work were viewed as female-only occupations. Students might also mention that women of the working class worked more often, while middle- and upper-class women were expected to attend to the domestic sphere.
saq_responses.part_b: Students can note the opportunity men gained to seek white collar occupations that involved science, engineering, law, construction, military service, and government service.
saq_responses.part_c: Students could describe the change in expectations on women. For example, women of the new middle class were expected to concentrate on the domestic sphere, while leaving the sphere of work outside the home increasingly to men. Students could also refer to the increasing restrictions on child labor and female labor (Factory Acts, Mines Act of 1842) that forced more women into some type of domestic work.

topics.title: The Concert of Europe and European Conservatism
topics.reflect_question: How was European political order reestablished and maintained in the period following Napoleon's defeat?
topics.reflect_response:
Political Order Maintained | Political Order Challenged
European leaders gather at Congress of Vienna after Napoleon's defeat and work to establish a balance of conservative powers in Europe | A member of a radical student organization murders the famous playwright August von Kotzebue
After the murder, Metternich brings about the Carlsbad Decrees, which aim to suppress nationalism within German states | German nationalism continues to grow
France restores its monarchy but limits it with a constitution | Charles X rules as absolute monarch, dissolving the governing body and increasing censorship
William I of the Kingdom of the Netherlands pursues autocratic rule | Belgium repudiates censorship and breaks away from the kingdom

saq_responses.part_a: Maistre was writing just after the period of the French Revolution, a period of domestic violence, and at a time when liberal ideas about human nature, social contract, and representation were spreading in Europe and the Americas.
saq_responses.part_b: Maistre was reacting to the changes in his society brought about by the Enlightenment, the Industrial Revolution, the French Revolution, and calls for republican forms of government. He wrote to defend tradition, religious authority, and rule by an elite.
saq_responses.part_c: Locke believed that government had legitimate authority because of a social contract among people who were governed, and he approved of constitutional monarchies. Students might cite Maistre's comments such as "History, however, which is experimental politics, demonstrates that a hereditary monarchy is the government, which is most stable, the happiest, and the most natural to man; and an elective monarchy, on the contrary, is the worst form of government known." They might also cite "God makes kings in the literal sense."

topics.title: Revolutions and Reactions
topics.reflect_question: How and why did various groups react against the existing order from 1815 to 1914?
topics.reflect_response:
Revolutions and Reactions | Outcomes of Revolutions and Reactions
Greeks demand independence from Ottoman Empire | Greece becomes independent, partly because other countries wanted to weaken the Ottoman Empire
Decembrists revolt in Russia | Nicholas I crushes the rebellion and creates harsh new laws
French people revolt against the autocratic Charles X | New king, Louis-Philippe, establishes constitutional monarchy and expands some men's voting rights
A group of young Polish soldiers rebels against Nicholas I and Russian control of Poland | Nicholas I crushes the rebellion and increases his control over Poland
French people revolt against Louis-Philippe for not being enough of a reformer | Louis-Philippe gives up the throne; France establishes a republic, but continued unrest leads to a new authoritarian government under Napoleon III
Prussians and those from other German states demand expanded rights | Frederick William IV crushes the rebellions
Members of ethnic groups in Austria demand self-rule; students riot | Metternich resigns; Habsburgs crush rebellions and create conservative monarchy
Radicals murder Alexander II of Russia | Alexander III reforms the economy but rejects liberal political reforms

saq_responses.part_a: He was among the European rulers who were holding on to despotism as demands for liberal reform increased. Because of their refusal to make changes, they risked disaster in the form of a revolution that could destroy their power.
saq_responses.part_b: Events in several countries demonstrated that despotic governments were able to crush liberal reforms. In Russia, the tsar crushed the Decembrists revolt. In France, the monarchy defeated the Revolution of 1830 and had to make only minor compromises. In the rebellion in Poland in 1830, Russian troops crushed the Poles. The Revolutions of 1848, at least in the short term, looked like failures because despots often consolidated their power.
saq_responses.part_c: Alexander II issued the Emancipation Manifesto (abolished serfdom), created the Zemstvo (council of elected officials), constructed railroads, and modernized the military. Alexander III continued the process of industrialization and improved education in commerce and technology.

topics.title: Ideologies of Change and Reform Movements
topics.reflect_question: How and why did different intellectual developments challenge the political and social order from 1815 to 1914?
topics.reflect_response:
Intellectual Development | Challenge to Political and Social Order

Popular sovereignty | Ordinary people rather than monarchs or nobles should hold most of the power in society
Utilitarianism | Laws should bring about the greatest happiness for the largest number of people

Anarchism | All forms of government should be destroyed
Syndicalism | After capitalism ends, labor unions should control everything

saq_responses.part_a: Students might explain how the Great Reform Act of 1832 in Great Britain allowed some prosperous men who owned little property—such as some merchants and factory owners—to vote. The repeal of the Corn Laws marked the growing power of the industrial middle class over agricultural interests.
saq_responses.part_b: Clara Zetkin wanted women to be able to vote so they could have a greater voice in social reforms to the issues caused by industrialization. She edited a socialist newspaper for women (Die Gleichheit) and pushed for an international workers' movement. Rosa Luxemburg believed workers had the right to rebel against oppressive governments. She formed the Spartacus League, a radical socialist group.
saq_responses.part_c: Henri Saint-Simon introduced the idea of utopian socialism, the belief that groups of people working together could create a better society. Based on Christian principles, Saint-Simon's ideas attracted a large following. These ideas of utopian societies were continued by Charles Fourier and Robert Owen, who established a community in New Lanark, Scotland.

topics.title: 19th-Century Social Reform
topics.reflect_question: What were the movements and calls for social reform that resulted from intellectual developments from 1815 to 1914?
topics.reflect_response:
Reform Movements | Goals of Movement
Development of mass political parties | Conservatives—protect interests of the wealthy; Liberals—favor social reforms that improve quality of life for ordinary people; Labor—protect the interests of working-class people; Marxist—bring about class revolution; Social Democrats—support workers and social change
Suffrage movements | Extend voting privileges to men without property, all men, or all women
Paris Commune | Anarchist workers tried to create a separate society for themselves
Women's rights movement | Voting rights, political activism, economic rights, right to make laws and policies, children's rights, end to human trafficking and sexual slavery, control over own property, higher education for women
Social gospel | Live the teachings of Christianity by providing food, shelter, and other help to workers and poor people
Temperance movement | Tax liquor; eventually ban the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages
Sunday School movement | Basic education for working-class children
Abolition movement | End the slave trade; make people aware of how they may be morally guilty if they buy or use products made by enslaved people; end slavery in colonies; end slavery everywhere

saq_responses.part_a: Possible answers: The tremendous growth of industry in Germany led to an influential working class; Bismarck introduced several social welfare reform measures in the 1870s and 1880s, and these reforms expanded the original social welfare reforms; the actions followed a trend that existed in other industrialized countries including France and Britain; the SPD at this point was the largest political party in Germany, and there was much support for their ideas.
saq_responses.part_b: The SDP was one of several mass political parties that emerged in Europe in the 19th century. It developed as a result of industrialization, which resulted in the development of the middle and working classes. These groups wanted to influence government, and through parties such as the SDP, they could.
saq_responses.part_c: The SDP opposed taxes that would fall most heavily on working people, and it supported taxes that would fall more heavily on wealthier people. This would support the argument of wealthier people not to support the SDP.

topics.title: Institutional Responses and Reform
topics.reflect_question: In what ways did governments and other institutions respond to challenges resulting from industrialization?
topics.reflect_response:
Governmental/Institutional Responses | Effects of Responses
Interventionism | Fewer laissez-faire attitudes and policies; more rules and policies that changed policing, prisons, urban planning, and education
Liberalism | Led to reforms in infrastructure, housing, public health, and public education; reduced the possibility of armed uprisings and widespread unrest
Expanded voting rights (for men) | Many ordinary people believed they had more of a say in politics
Prison reform | Separation of men and women in prisons; more humane treatment for prisoners
Large-scale urban renewal projects | Improved water, lighting, and traffic flow for Paris, Vienna, and other cities
Education reforms | More children in school; higher literacy rates; greater sense of nationalism

saq_responses.part_a: Paris was suffering from the effects of the Industrial Revolution. Its population was growing so it was overcrowded and dangerously filthy. Factories were polluting the air, and increased commerce made the narrow streets crowded.
saq_responses.part_b: France experienced a period of peace and stability in the 1850s, so it could more easily afford the cost of rebuilding the city.
saq_responses.part_c: Since it is a painting, it reflects the views of the artist, who might desire to emphasize a particular aspect of life rather than show the city as accurately as possible. Since the painting was completed in 1898, it might show changes that occurred after Haussmann's time.

topics.title: Causation in the Age of Industrialization
skill_responses: Innovations and technological developments caused the advancement of manufacturing, transportation, and communications in Europe. Industry changed daily life in Britain first, then Europe, especially the heavily industrialized locations. Social classes changed into an industrial working class, a professional middle class, and a wealthy upper class of business owners. The changes to daily life brought on by the Age of Industrialization also influenced political ideologies and governments, as reform movements grew in response to the new technologies.

The Industrial Revolution and political upheavals caused new political ideologies to develop and take hold in Europe during the 19th century. Conservatism was one of the ideologies that was a response to the tremendous changes brought on by industrialization and political revolutions. Liberalism was an ideology that was a response to traditional status quo. European liberals wanted quick reforms to political systems to match the societal changes caused by industrialization.

topics.title: Contextualizing 19th-Century Perspectives and Political Developments
skill_responses: By 1815, Europe's rising industrial working class and rising urban middle class had new ideologies and wanted more freedoms and new political structures. The resulting romantic movement started nationalism, which is the belief that people should be joined for a purpose based on common ties of language, ethnicity, culture, and history.

European imperialism came to be when industrialization greatly boosted Europe's economy. In the 19th century, strong European nations competed with each other to control colonies such as Africa and Asia.

topics.title: Nationalism
topics.reflect_question: How did the development and spread of nationalism affect Europe from 1815 to 1914?
topics.reflect_response:
Advocate for Nationalism | Effects of Advocate's Efforts
Johann Gottlieb Fichte | Espoused Germany's special importance; fueled future German chauvinists
Giuseppe Mazzini | Founded Young Italy movement that led small but unsuccessful uprisings; inspired future Italian nationalists
Camillo di Cavour | Helped achieve liberal constitution in Piedmont-Sardinia; led Italian middle class in their goal of Italian reunification
Otto von Bismarck | Led German unification movement as foreign minister and then prime minister of Prussia; used selected liberal policies along with an aggressive foreign policy (starting wars to drum up nationalistic feelings) to push for a Prussian-dominated Germany
Theodore Herzl | Founded political Zionism; considered one of the nation of Israel's founders

saq_responses.part_a: According to Herzl, the Dreyfus Affair caused him to become an advocate for Zionism because it showed the persistence of anti-Semitism in European society, even in countries where many Jews had seemed to have assimilated. However, he might have been a supporter before Zionism.
saq_responses.part_b: Herzl's advocacy of Zionism occurred at the same time as a political form of nationalism was growing in Europe. Hungarians and Slavs wanted self-determination, while Italians and Germans wanted unification.
saq_responses.part_c: Herzl was responding to anti-Semitism—discrimination and persecution against Jews. In contrast, Bismarck was not responding to attacks on Germans. He wanted to unite people in order to strengthen Prussia. In addition, Herzl did not have a clear territory in mind for a Jewish state, while Bismarck knew the land he wanted in a German state.

topics.title: National Unification and Diplomatic Tensions
topics.reflect_question: What factors resulted in Italian unification and German unification?
topics.reflect_response:
Factors in Italian Unification | Factors in German Unification
Italian nationalism | German nationalism
Cavour's diplomacy (realpolitik) and deceit | Bismarck's use of realpolitik and deceit
Alliance with France | Wars with Denmark, Austria, and France
War with Austria |
Revolutionary movements |
Garibaldi's rebel army of Red Shirts |
historical_perspectives: In one way, Renan's theory about nationalism best describes the unification of Italy. The regions that made up the new country had not been united since the age of classical Rome, and they had often been rivals with each other. For them to unite, they had to forget all that had separated them.

In one way, Anderson's theory about nationalism best describes the unification of Germany. It was led by elites, such as Bismarck and the Prussian nobles. In another way, German unification represented the ideas of Michelet. Cultural traits, such as language and literature, united people across political boundaries.
In one way, Michelet's theory about nationalism best describes the conflicts in the Balkans. Various cultural groups fought for self-determination against the rule of the Habsburgs or the Ottomans.

saq_responses.part_a: Students could refer to Russia's desires to take advantage of the weakening Ottoman Empire by expanding southward into territory controlled by the Ottoman Empire as a cause of the Crimean War. Another cause was Britain's need to preserve the Ottoman Empire in order to keep the Russian navy trapped in the Black Sea and prevent Russia from becoming strong enough to threaten the European balance of power. A third reason could explain how France tried to gain influence in the Ottoman Empire by becoming the protector of Ottoman Christians, a move that Russia resisted.
saq_responses.part_b: Among the effects of the Crimean War were huge casualties—Russia alone suffered approximately 450,000 casualties. Students could explain how Russia's navy was bottled up in the Black Sea for decades. When Russian leaders realized they had fallen behind the Western European states in industrialization and placed a new emphasis on economic development, Alexander II was forced to liberalize society in order to forestall peasant unrest, including the abolition of serfdom in 1861.
saq_responses.part_c: A long-term effect of the Crimean War was the alliance of Sardinia with France. The Crimean War thus paved the way for first Italian, and then later German, unification. In addition, students could explain how Russia became embittered toward European powers, especially Austria, for not coming to its aid during the war.

topics.title: Darwinism, Social Darwinism
topics.reflect_question: How did Darwin's theories influence scientific and social developments from 1815 to 1914?
topics.reflect_response:
Darwin's Theories | Influence
Theory of evolution: species change, or evolve | Initially shocked Victorian society
Natural selection: some traits help individuals survive | Appealed to rising class of professional scientists
Humans are descended from primate ancestors | Inspired the idea of Social Darwinism, "survival of the fittest," which was used to justify the subjugation of people in Africa and Asia

saq_responses.part_a: Scientific ideas spread easily in Europe between 1859 and 1872. The rise of nationalism, the frequent use of censorship, and fear of controversy did not prevent Darwin's ideas being translated.
saq_responses.part_b: On the Origins of Species was first translated in countries where the Industrial Revolution was well-established, regardless of whether the country was dominated by Roman Catholics, Protestants, or Orthodox.
saq_responses.part_c: Both Darwin and Enlightenment thinkers relied on observation and reason more than religious beliefs and tradition to develop their ideas.

topics.title: The Age of Progress and Modernity
topics.reflect_question: How did science and other intellectual disciplines develop and change from 1815 to 1914?
topics.reflect_response:
Development | Impact of Development
Materialism held that everything is matter. | Marx's ideas focused on physical processes.
Positivism held that science alone provides knowledge. | Marx's ideas were positivist because he grounded them in facts.
Modernism avoided committing to any system that would stifle creativity. | Modernists pioneered new ideas in psychology and political theory, as well as in science: Freud founded psychoanalysis; Einstein came up with a theory of relativity; Planck's quantum theory resulted in quantum mechanics
Irrationalism focused on impulses rather than reason. | Irrationalist philosophers such as Nietzsche, Sorel, and Bergson influenced artists and politicians.

saq_responses.part_a: Comte was writing in France in the mid-19th century, a period when life was changing much faster than it had in previous centuries because of the Industrial Revolution and of political upheavals such as the revolutions in France in 1789, 1791, and 1830. The Enlightenment had challenged explanations of the natural world and of human society.
saq_responses.part_b: Students could provide any of several possible answers. Scientists such as Darwin rejected the theological explanations of natural phenomena and proposed explanations based on observation and reason. Political thinkers such as Rousseau and Burke rejected the theological explanation for the power of a monarch (the divine right of kings) and proposed an explanation based on human decisions (the social contract). Historians such as Marx were viewing history as a series of stages that people progressed through.
saq_responses.part_c: Students could provide any of several possible answers. Irrationalists such as Nietzsche, Sorel, and Bergson, and psychoanalysts such as Freud, explored ways that people did not make decisions based on reason. In culture, Romanticism and nationalism relied on emotion rather than reason. Events such as the Crimean War, Italian unification, and German unification were shaped by theological differences among ethnic groups.

topics.title: New Imperialism: Motivations and Methods
topics.reflect_question: What were the motivations and technological advances that helped advance European imperialism from 1815 to 1914?
topics.reflect_response:
Motivations | Technological Advances
Industrial powers wanted access to raw materials for their factories. | Advances in weaponry, including the development of new types of rifles and machine guns, made it possible to subjugate large populations with fewer soldiers.
Industrial powers wanted new markets for their manufactured goods and sources for new investments. | Advances in medicine allowed Europeans to be vaccinated against many diseases and provided cures for others, such as malaria.
Overseas empires gave nations power, prestige, and strategic advantages. | Improvements in transportation, such as the railroad, steamship, and the Suez Canal, allowed Europeans to transport goods and personnel more quickly and efficiently.
Imperialists considered colonization to be a mission to help civilize Africans and Asians. | Advances in communication, such as the telegraph and undersea cable, allowed European nations to communicate with their overseas empires.
 | The development of photography allowed European powers to document their colonies. It also provided a way for activists to document atrocities.

saq_responses.part_a: The Industrial Revolution increased production and lowered the cost of quinine, just as it had done for textiles and other goods. This made quinine widely available.
saq_responses.part_b: When quinine became widely available, it aided imperialism by making it safer for Europeans to settle in and colonize tropical regions.
saq_responses.part_c: The author focuses on how quinine has become less expensive and easier to obtain, which has benefited the "vast populations inhabiting malarious districts." In this passage, he does not address the costs to people of increased imperialism.

topics.reflect_question: How did imperialism affect European and non-European societies?
topics.reflect_response:
Effects on European Societies | Effects on Non-European Societies
Increased domestic and international tensions | Fashoda Crisis between the British and French in Africa
Strained European alliances | Conflict between Germany and France over control of Morocco
Critics began to debate the ethics and economic value of imperialism: The Congo Reform Association led to widespread condemnation of Leopold II's Congo regime. J. A. Hobson argued that imperialism made the European economy dependent on unstable markets. Lenin said imperialism would inspire a global revolution against capitalism. | Zulus resisted British rule but were quelled
 | Ethiopia successfully defended itself against an Italian attempt to take over
 | The Sepoy Rebellion in India resulted in the British government taking over control from the East India Company
 | Congress Party formed to fight for Indian independence
 | Boxer Rebellion in China opposed Western influences in China but was put down by a coalition of Western nations (and Japan)
 | Japan modernized in order to protect itself from industrialized powers

saq_responses.part_a: Students could support Headrick's technologically based argument for New Imperialism by identifying the role of various new technologies, such as the Maxim gun, steamboat, and telegraph. For example, the Maxim gun allowed smaller European militaries to defeat larger native forces. Responses may also note how the telegraph and submarine cables allowed colonies to quickly communicate with the mother country. A third possibility to support Headrick's argument is to address the ability of steamboats to navigate African and Asian waterways like the Niger River with greater ease.
saq_responses.part_b: Students may refute Headrick's technologically based argument by addressing the impact of capitalism on New Imperialism. For example, as the middle class rose and industrial production increased, the industrialists sought new markets to sell European goods as well as new territories to acquire the needed raw materials for industrialization. Responses could also note the role of the government in New Imperialism as nationalism caused nations to compete for territory in order to demonstrate their strength and prestige. For example, students could refer to the actions of Great Britain and Germany in Africa.
saq_responses.part_c: Students could support Headrick's argument by describing how the Age of Exploration also relied on technology. Students may note the role of the caravel in navigating the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Students might also reference the need for the compass and astrolabe in navigation. Another possibility could be to address the use of muskets and cannons in providing a military advantage against the Aztecs and Incas.

topics.title: 19th-Century Culture and Arts
topics.reflect_question: What were the continuities and changes in European artistic expression from 1815 to 1914?
topics.reflect_response:

topics.title: Continuity and Changes in an Age of Global Conflict
skill_responses: The losers of World War I were forced to pay reparations for the damages caused by the war, even as European currencies had declined in value due to the war. In addition, the same countries were in massive debt from the war and needed money to rebuild from war damage during the 1920s. Then in 1929, the U.S. stock market crashed, setting off the Great Depression, which quickly spread through Europe. Unemployment rose, causing radical political responses and destabilizing many democracies in western Europe.

In a democracy, individuals are free to elect government members and develop their individual self-interests through a capitalist economy. In communism, the working class would own the means of production and individuals would avoid being oppressed laborers. Individuals would eventually have no need for a governing power. In fascism, the lives of individuals and the economy were controlled by a strong central government headed by a dictator.

topics.title: Contextualizing Cold War and Contemporary Europe
skill_responses: At the end of World War II, the United States wanted democracy to spread throughout the world, while the Soviet Union wanted communism. In addition, the United States and the Soviet Union had been affected much differently by World War II. The Soviets had suffered huge casualties and destruction of cities and economies. The contrast in war experiences caused the superpowers to have contrasting postwar plans. The Soviet Union's postwar plans included controlling Eastern Europe and dividing Germany in order to protect itself from military threats from the United States and Western Europe. The United States' postwar plans included rebuilding Eastern Europe's governments and keeping Germany whole, believing this would stabilize all and create new markets for U.S. goods.

When World War II ended, Soviet troops occupied a line of countries along their western border that came to be known as the Iron Curtain: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, and Albania. The Soviets secured or installed communist governments in those countries to create a buffer zone to protect the Soviet Union from invasion from Western Europe. The United States responded by adopting a policy of containment in an effort to block Soviet threats to Eastern Europe and to stop any further expansion of communism. This Cold War that followed between the Soviet Union and the United States put the rest of the world under pressure to choose a side. The context for the end of the Cold War came about in the 1980s, when the Soviet Union no longer was matching the United States' aggression in the Cold War. Meanwhile, Eastern Europe was pushing against Soviet control, and by 1989, the Berlin Wall fell. Soviet attempts at internal reforms failed.
