Communist and socialist countries promoted women's rights | Women made some progress but often suffered under a double burden, with more responsibilities and fewer rewards than men
Women became elected or appointed leaders of political parties and entire countries | Although female elected leaders often disagreed with one another, many women sought improved conditions for themselves, children, and men

saq_responses.part_a: Students could refer to high birth rates and large family size that made it difficult for women to escape traditional nurturing roles to pursue higher education. Ongoing societal pressures for women to be primary housekeepers and caregivers for children also caused low postsecondary participation in education in Europe prior to 1950.
saq_responses.part_b: Students could explain long-term declines in birth rates beginning in the 1960s freed many women from the demands of childcare, enabling them to pursue higher education. Students could also refer to the advent of the feminist movement that encouraged many more women to pursue higher education. Women were inspired by the civil rights movements in the U.S. and anti-Vietnam war demonstrations across the U.S. and Europe to aggressively seek expanded educational opportunities. Writers such as Simone de Beauvoir (The Second Sex, 1949) examined causes of the limited opportunities for women and encouraged women to assert their rights, including the right of higher education.
saq_responses.part_c: Students could point out the connection between divorce rates and female participation in postsecondary education. For example, as divorce rates began to increase in the 1960s, more women entered the workforce, and a considerable number of them returned to school to acquire employable skills or credentials.

topics.title: Decolonization
topics.reflect_question: What were the various ways in which colonial groups around the world sought independence from colonizers in the 20th and 21st centuries?
topics.reflect_response:
Efforts for Independence | Results
Wilson advocated for self-determination | Self-determination was not part of the League of Nations charter
Indian people volunteered for military and support services in World War I | Indian National Congress sought independence; Britain made minor concessions but kept India as part of the British Empire
France used many of its colonists as soldiers and factory workers in wartime | France refused to grant its colonies independence
League of Nations established mandate system after World War I | Great Britain and France controlled more territory (and oil) in the Middle East
World War II weakened colonizing nations | India, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Indonesia achieved independence
Algerian nationalists warred with the French | Algeria gained independence
In the 1960s and 1970s, Britain, France, Belgium, and Portugal gave up direct control of their colonies | Angola and several other African nations gained independence
Countries decolonized | Former colonies often depended on former colonizers for funding, technology, and jobs

saq_responses.part_a: Students might explain how the USSR and PRC encouraged rebellion in the developing world against European colonial powers, specifically supporting Communist-led independence movements with aid in Algeria, Egypt, and other places. Students might also explain how the United States used its influence to pressure European states to grant independence to colonies (the Netherlands in Indonesia and Spain in Morocco).
saq_responses.part_b: Students could explain how the economic toll of World War II caused several European states to grant independence to former colonies. For example, former Axis colonies, such as Italy's colony in Libya, were granted independence. Former French colonies in northwest Africa that had been administered by Vichy France during the war were also granted independence after the conclusion of World War II. Students could also discuss how the involvement of numerous colonial troops, who fought for Allied forces during the war, gave them moral claim to independence as well as exposed weaknesses of the European militaries.
saq_responses.part_c: Students could refer to Algeria and the long, bloody civil war with France. Many of those who had remained loyal to France were killed or forced to flee. Another result of decolonization would be to note sub-Saharan Africa. For example, many states were formed from the former colonies, often forcing groups to live together who had never done so, leading to genocide. A third possible result could explain that even though India became free, religious disputes remained and caused further division of the country.

topics.title: The European Union
topics.reflect_question: How has the formation and existence of the European Union influenced economic developments from the end of World War II to the present?
topics.reflect_response:
EU-related Event | Effects on Economic Development
United States requires European countries to use postwar development funds cooperatively | Formation of OEEC and ECSC
Need for consistent rules and tax collection in European countries | Establishment of European Parliament
Desire for free trade and free movement between countries | Formation of EEC; passage of Single European Act
Expansion of EU | Greater economic power but more controversies within EU
Brexit | Concerns and debates over EU's strength and survival

saq_responses.part_a: Immediately after World War II, leaders such as Robert Schuman of France believed that closer economic integration of Europe, particularly between France and Germany, would promote peace. These ideas prompted leaders to create several organizations in the following decades, including the Organization for European Economic Cooperation, the European Coal and Steel Community, the European Parliament, and the European Economic Community. The last of these changed its name to the European Union.
saq_responses.part_b: Increased economic integration in Western and Central Europe allowed for tax-free trade among businesses, easier travel across borders for work and tourism, simpler financial transactions, and more effective addressing of problems such as pollution.
saq_responses.part_c: Economic integration contributed to the most peaceful period in Europe in many centuries. This peace provided the stability that led to great prosperity throughout the region.

topics.title: Migration and Immigration
topics.reflect_question: What have been the causes and effects of changes to migration within and immigration to Europe from the end of World War II to the present?
topics.reflect_response:
Causes | Effects
Holocaust and repression | Death or emigration of millions of Jews
Decolonization and economic opportunities | Immigration to Europe from India, Pakistan, the Caribbean, and Africa
Labor shortages in Europe | Guest worker programs brought immigrants to Europe
Immigration of non-Christians | Increase in European residents and citizens who practice Islam, Hinduism, or Buddhism
Changes to climate and ecology in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East | Increased immigration to Europe, where climate is more moderate
Economic downturns | Increased popularity of anti-immigrant, anti-Muslim political parties

saq_responses.part_a: The percentage of nonnational residents from other EU countries and from non-EU countries is similar for most countries. Only Estonia has a much higher percentage from non-EU countries.
saq_responses.part_b: Many immigrants to Europe come from the Middle East or Africa, so Malta would be closer than would most of the continent.
saq_responses.part_c: While Austria had a higher percentage of immigrants than did Europe overall, its percentage was similar to that of its neighbor Germany, and more of its nonnational residents came from other EU countries than from non-EU countries.

topics.title: Technology
topics.reflect_question: How have innovations and advances in technology influenced cultural and intellectual developments from 1914 to the present?
topics.reflect_response:
Innovations and Technological Advances | Influence on Cultural and Intellectual Developments
Increase in average lifespan | Questions of how best to support and care for an aging population
Improvements in medicine | Cultural, moral, and religious questions related to birth control, abortion, eugenics, fertility, genetics, and stem cells
New military technologies | Anxiety over industrialized warfare and nuclear proliferation

saq_responses.part_a: Students might identify the phrase "happily led to me being born" and note that Brown says her mother was depressed because she could not have children and that the doctors suggested she take the middle name of Joy because she would bring joy to many people.
saq_responses.part_b: Some procedures and technology that also raised moral questions were birth control, abortion, eugenics, genetic research, and stem cell research.
saq_responses.part_c: One general moral concern was that IVF intervenes in the basic processes of life, an activity that some people find violates their religious or ethical beliefs.

topics.title: Globalization
topics.reflect_question: What have been the technological and cultural causes of increasing European globalization from 1914 to the present?
topics.reflect_response:
Technological Causes | Cultural Causes
World War II–related production needs ended, so countries and businesses were able to focus on producing consumer goods | Societies began to become more consumption-oriented, seeking out varied and inexpensive options from around the world
Increased consumerism and energy use contributed to some environmental crises; many people across the world became more concerned about the environment | Environment-focused Green Parties formed in many countries in Northern Europe and Western Europe

saq_responses.part_a: The consumer culture of post-World War II Europe was a continuation of the trends toward mass production and mass consumption that began with the Industrial Revolution in the 18th century. Workers were becoming more productive, and consumers could obtain more goods at lower prices.
saq_responses.part_b: The consumer culture of post-World War II Europe was a change from earlier periods because it was done on a greater scale, it relied more on electricity for power, and it used more synthetic materials such as plastics. In addition, it was more heavily shaped by U.S. movies, television shows, music, video games, and other technology.
saq_responses.part_c: Radios and televisions gave people in rural and urban areas access to the same entertainment experiences and news—and at the same time. Automobiles made transportation between rural and urban areas easier than ever before. Computers and the Internet connected people, not just in rural and urban areas but around the world.

topics.title: 20th- and 21st-Century Culture, Art, and Demographic Trends
topics.reflect_question: How and why has European culture changed from the end of World War II to the present?
topics.reflect_response:
How European Culture Changed | Why European Culture Changed
New philosophies | Upheaval after the horrors of war
Decline of religiousness in some areas of Europe | More people lived in cities instead of church-centered towns; scientific discoveries gave people hope; totalitarian governments wanted to erase religion or greatly reduce its power
New ideas in visual art, architecture, literature, and theater | Rejections of old ideas and standards; in some cases, increased interest in the subconscious
Influence of American popular culture | Europeans reacted to new ideas and art forms from another consumerist society
Development of a consumer culture | Technological innovations that made daily life easier, safer, and more pleasant
Struggle for civil rights by various groups | Groups tended to learn from and inspire one another

saq_responses.part_a: Students could note the importance of the Second Vatican Council or Pope John XXIII's implantation of reforms that appealed to a more secular world. For example, students could explain the role of the council in allowing the mass to be said in vernacular languages rather than Latin, making it more accessible. Students could also address how the council encouraged laypeople to participate more in the mass and the church. Students could also discuss the reconciliation between Catholics and Jews, Catholics and Muslims, or Catholics and Eastern Orthodox believers.
saq_responses.part_b: Students could discuss how a growing number of people in Eastern and Western Europe embraced secular tradition and moved away from organized religion after World War II. Students could address the growing Muslim minority in France and Russia from 1950–1991. Students may note that 75 percent of Europeans still identified as Christian, proving that organized religion was still relevant.
saq_responses.part_c: Students could explain the impact of communism on the role of organized religion in Eastern Europe. While Western Europeans became more secular by choice, communism repressed religious freedom for Eastern Europeans, leading to the decline of organized religion. Students could discuss the role of organized religions in East Germany and Poland in shaping resistance to the Soviet Union in the 1980s. Students may also explore the role of Pope John Paul II in Poland.

topics.title: Continuity and Change in the 20th and 21st Centuries
skill_responses: The total wars—World War I and World War II—affected all Europeans, destroying many lives, homes, cities, and economies. The Cold War affected Europe with global political instability. During this time there was also nationalist violence and ethnic conflicts within European nations.

Many people's confidence in science, technology, reason, and religion disappeared. A sense of anxiety came out of the global conflicts and affected many Europeans. From this challenge to traditional everyday life came new intellectual and cultural movements from new voices, including postmodernism—the idea that no objective truths exist. Societies became more liberal, and civil rights movements became popular.
